nodes.label: Jalayirids, Muzaffarids, Karts
nodes.full: The Ilkhanate's collapse produced three durable regional successor dynasties — Jalayirids in Iraq and Azerbaijan, Muzaffarids in Fars and Kerman, and the long-established Karts in Herat — each ruling as effectively independent Persian-administered states until Timur's campaigns absorbed or destroyed them one after another in the 1380s.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, continuation of Rashid al-Din's Jami al-Tawarikh, on the post-Ilkhanid successor states.

nodes.label: Timur subdues the successors
nodes.full: Timur eliminated the Karts, Muzaffarids and Jalayirids as independent powers in successive campaigns through the 1380s, each conquest marked by the systematic destruction of any city that resisted and the incorporation of the survivors' skilled craftsmen and scholars into his own capital at Samarkand.
nodes.src: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama, on Timur's Iranian campaigns.

nodes.label: Sack of Isfahan
nodes.full: After Isfahan's population rose up and killed the tax officials Timur had installed, his army retook the city and reportedly built towers from the skulls of tens of thousands of its inhabitants — a calculated act of terror, whatever the precise casualty figures, meant to ensure no other city under his rule would consider similar resistance.
nodes.src: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama, on the sack of Isfahan, with the same caution warranted for all medieval casualty figures.

nodes.label: Toll of Timur campaigns
nodes.full: As with the earlier Mongol conquest, court-commissioned chronicles' casualty figures for cities like Isfahan almost certainly exceed what the cities' actual populations could have supplied — but modern historians agree the underlying pattern of mass killing, forced deportation of skilled populations to Samarkand, and genuine demographic collapse across much of Iran was real, whatever the precise numbers.
nodes.src: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama; modern demographic critique of medieval Timurid-era casualty figures.

nodes.label: Timur
nodes.full: Ruling from Samarkand as an emir rather than claiming the title of khan himself, Timur built an empire through nearly continuous campaigning across Iran, Central Asia, India, the Caucasus and Anatolia — a military career whose sheer geographic range and reported brutality made him, alongside Genghis Khan, one of the two conquerors most feared in the historical memory of the entire region he crossed.
nodes.src: Nizam al-Din Shami and Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, both court-commissioned Zafarnama ('Book of Victory') biographies of Timur.

nodes.label: Extractive conquest state
nodes.full: Timur's administration prioritised the extraction of plunder, tribute and skilled craftsmen from conquered territory to enrich Samarkand over any sustained investment in provincial government — a model of rule built for continuous campaigning that left most conquered regions, including much of Iran, administratively neglected outside the capital itself.
nodes.src: Comparative institutional analysis of Timurid conquest-era administration versus later consolidation under Shah Rukh.

nodes.label: Monuments at Samarkand
nodes.full: Timur rebuilt Samarkand as an imperial capital worthy of his conquests, commissioning the vast Bibi-Khanym congregational mosque and his own eventual mausoleum, the Gur-e Amir — buildings whose scale and ornamental ambition drew explicitly on architectural traditions and craftsmen looted from across his conquered territories, including Iran, Iraq and India.
nodes.src: Bibi-Khanym Mosque and Gur-e Amir mausoleum, Samarkand, extant structures.

nodes.label: Delhi and Ankara
nodes.full: Timur's sack of Delhi in 1398 and his decisive defeat and capture of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402 demonstrated a genuinely intercontinental military reach — the Ankara victory in particular delayed the Ottoman Empire's own rise by a full decade of internal succession crisis, with consequences felt as far away as Constantinople and the courts of Christian Europe.
nodes.src: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama; Ottoman chronicle traditions on the aftermath of Ankara.

nodes.label: A conqueror reshapes Eurasia
nodes.full: Timur's campaigns touched territory from Delhi to Moscow to Damascus to Ankara within a single reign, delaying the Ottoman Empire's rise by a decade, devastating the Golden Horde's power in the Russian steppe, and redrawing the political map of Iran, Central Asia and northern India — a geographic range of consequence matched by very few individual military careers in world history.
nodes.src: Comparative assessment of Timur's campaigns' geopolitical consequences across Eurasia.

nodes.label: Shah Rukh and Timurid Renaissance
nodes.full: Timur's son Shah Rukh moved the dynastic capital to Herat and governed through consolidation and cultural patronage rather than further conquest, presiding over what art and literary historians now call the Timurid Renaissance — the era's most sustained flowering of Persian manuscript painting, architecture and poetry.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, Zubdat al-Tawarikh, on Shah Rukh's reign.

nodes.label: Settled administration
nodes.full: Shah Rukh reversed his father's extractive approach, investing in provincial administration, agricultural restoration and religious and cultural patronage across the Timurid domains — a consolidative style of rule that let Herat flourish as a genuine cultural capital rather than merely a treasury for continuous war.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, Zubdat al-Tawarikh, on Shah Rukh's administrative priorities.

nodes.label: Agricultural restoration
nodes.full: Shah Rukh's administration invested in restoring irrigation infrastructure and resettling agricultural land depopulated by his father's campaigns — a direct policy response to the specific economic damage Timur's own conquests had inflicted on the very regions his son now needed to govern productively.
nodes.src: Hafiz-i Abru, Zubdat al-Tawarikh, on Shah Rukh's agricultural policy.

nodes.label: Trade recovers
nodes.full: After the destruction of Timur's own campaigns, the relative stability of Shah Rukh's and his successors' reigns allowed Silk Road commerce through Herat and Samarkand to recover substantially — the same cities that had suffered worst under Timur's conquest becoming, within a generation, major beneficiaries of the peace his heirs maintained.
nodes.src: Comparative economic history of Timurid-era Central Asian and Iranian trade recovery.

nodes.label: Gawhar Shad Herat complex
nodes.full: Shah Rukh's wife Gawhar Shad personally commissioned a major mosque and madrasa complex at Herat and a companion complex at Mashhad, among the finest surviving examples of Timurid religious architecture — monumental building projects funded and directed by a royal woman in her own name, not merely attributed to her husband's reign.
nodes.src: Gawhar Shad Mosque, Herat and Mashhad, extant and partially surviving structures.

nodes.label: Gawhar Shad independent patronage
nodes.full: Gawhar Shad commissioned, funded and directed major architectural projects at Herat and Mashhad in her own name and by her own initiative rather than merely as an extension of her husband Shah Rukh's rule — documented evidence of a royal woman exercising substantial independent authority over resources and public monuments in her own right.
nodes.src: Gawhar Shad Mosque foundation inscriptions, Herat and Mashhad.

nodes.label: Herat tile and dome technique
nodes.full: Gawhar Shad's mosque and madrasa complex employed sophisticated tile-mosaic (kashi) techniques and structural innovations in dome and minaret construction that Timurid builders had refined across successive projects at Samarkand, Herat and Mashhad, representing a mature and confident engineering tradition rather than experimental early efforts.
nodes.src: Gawhar Shad Mosque complex, Herat, extant and partially surviving structure.

nodes.label: Embassy to the Ming
nodes.full: Shah Rukh sent a formal embassy to the Ming Chinese court, whose member Ghiyath al-din Naqqash wrote a detailed eyewitness account of Ming China — court ceremony, cities, technology — that survives as one of the richest firsthand Persian descriptions of Ming-era China produced by any foreign visitor.
nodes.src: Ghiyath al-din Naqqash's travel account, preserved via Hafiz-i Abru's Zubdat al-Tawarikh.

nodes.label: Ulugh Beg
nodes.full: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg governed Samarkand for decades as a scholar-prince before briefly holding the full imperial throne, more celebrated in his own lifetime and ever since for his astronomical observatory than for his short and troubled reign, which ended when his own son had him assassinated.
nodes.src: Abd al-Razzaq Samarqandi, Matla al-Sa'dayn, on Ulugh Beg's reign and death.

nodes.label: Ulugh Beg star catalogue
nodes.full: Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand, equipped with one of the largest astronomical instruments ever built for naked-eye observation, produced a catalogue of over a thousand stars with a positional accuracy that remained among the best available anywhere in the world for the following two centuries.
nodes.src: Ulugh Beg, Zij-i Sultani (the Samarkand star catalogue and astronomical tables).

nodes.label: Samarkand observatory
nodes.full: Ulugh Beg's observatory housed a giant sextant partially cut into a hillside, among the largest astronomical measuring instruments ever constructed for naked-eye observation — an engineering solution to instrument-scale precision problems that pre-telescopic astronomy anywhere else in the world rarely attempted to match.
nodes.src: Ulugh Beg Observatory remains, Samarkand, rediscovered by archaeological excavation in 1908.

nodes.label: Husayn Bayqara and late Herat
nodes.full: The last major Timurid ruler, Sultan Husayn Bayqara presided over Herat's final and most celebrated cultural flowering — the painter Bihzad, the poet Jami and the statesman-poet Ali-Shir Nava'i were all active at his court — even as the dynasty's political and military position across the wider region continued to erode toward the Uzbek conquest that would end Timurid rule in Herat within a few years of this folio's close.
nodes.src: Khvandamir, Habib al-Siyar, on Sultan Husayn Bayqara's court and its cultural figures.

nodes.label: Bihzad
nodes.full: Working at Sultan Husayn Bayqara's Herat court, Kamal ud-Din Bihzad brought Persian manuscript illustration to a level of psychological nuance, spatial complexity and individualised characterisation that later generations across the Persian, Ottoman and Mughal worlds treated as the standard against which all subsequent miniature painting was measured.
nodes.src: Bihzad-attributed manuscript paintings, Topkapi Palace Museum, British Library and other collections.

nodes.label: Jami
nodes.full: Nur al-Din Jami's mystical and narrative poetry, produced at the Herat court under Sultan Husayn Bayqara's patronage, is widely regarded by literary historians as the last major work in the classical Persian poetic tradition running back through Hafez, Sa'di and Rumi — a tradition whose greatest innovations, by broad critical consensus, effectively closed with his generation.
nodes.src: Jami, Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones) and other collected works.

nodes.label: Chagatai Turkish at Herat
nodes.full: Ali-Shir Nava'i's championing of Chagatai Turkish as a literary language equal in dignity to Persian at Sultan Husayn Bayqara's court reflected the genuinely bilingual Turco-Persian culture of the late Timurid elite — Central Asian Turkic and Iranian Persian literary traditions developing side by side within the same royal patronage system rather than in separate worlds.
nodes.src: Ali-Shir Nava'i, Muhakamat al-Lughatayn (Judgement of the Two Languages), explicitly comparing Chagatai Turkish and Persian as literary media.

nodes.label: Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu
nodes.full: Two rival Turkmen tribal confederations, the Black Sheep (Qara Qoyunlu) and White Sheep (Aq Qoyunlu), fought each other and the Timurids for control of western Iran and Iraq across more than a century — Uzun Hasan's Aq Qoyunlu eventually dominated the region at its peak before its own decline opened the way for the rising Safavid movement to seize power in 1501.
nodes.src: Fazlallah ibn Ruzbihan Khunji, Tarikh-i Alam-Ara-yi Amini, on the Aq Qoyunlu confederation.

nodes.label: Uzun Hasan defeats Jahan Shah
nodes.full: Uzun Hasan's Aq Qoyunlu forces decisively defeated and killed the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahan Shah, ending the long Black Sheep–White Sheep rivalry in the White Sheep's favour and briefly making the Aq Qoyunlu confederation the dominant power across western Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia.
nodes.src: Fazlallah ibn Ruzbihan Khunji, Tarikh-i Alam-Ara-yi Amini, on the defeat of Jahan Shah.

nodes.label: Battle of Otlukbeli
nodes.full: Ottoman sultan Mehmed II's army, equipped with far more extensive artillery than Uzun Hasan's forces, decisively defeated the Aq Qoyunlu at Otlukbeli — checking White Sheep expansion into Anatolia for good and confirming the Ottomans, rather than any Turkmen confederation, as the dominant power on Iran's northwestern frontier going forward.
nodes.src: Ottoman chronicle traditions (e.g. Tursun Beg) on the Battle of Otlukbeli.

nodes.label: Safavid order quiet beginnings
nodes.full: The Safaviyya Sufi order, founded by Safi al-Din Ardabili as an orthodox Sunni mystical brotherhood, spent its first century as a respected but politically unremarkable religious institution at Ardabil — its later transformation into a militant, explicitly Shia movement under Junayd and Haydar, and finally into the Safavid Empire itself under Ismail I in 1501, still lay decades in this folio's future.
nodes.src: Ahmad ibn al-Khwafi, Safwat al-Safa, an early hagiographic account of Safi al-Din Ardabili.

nodes.label: Sunni orthodoxy
nodes.full: Both the Timurid dynasty and the rival Turkmen confederations remained officially Sunni throughout this period, patronising orthodox madrasas and Sufi orders of the kind the still-Sunni Safaviyya itself represented — a religious landscape that would be upended within a generation of this folio's close by the openly Shia Safavid state.
nodes.src: Comparative religious patronage evidence across Timurid and Turkmen court records.

nodes.label: The vacuum Timur left
nodes.full: Timur's empire fractured within decades of his death into a settled but politically weakened Timurid remnant centred on Herat and a series of Turkmen and, eventually, a new Safavid power contesting western Iran — the conqueror's vast territorial reach proved far easier to seize than to institutionalise into a lasting unified state.
nodes.src: Comparative political geography of the fragmenting post-Timurid Iranian world, 15th century.
